doc.title: Vince DiMartino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 8, 2025

title: Band director Edward DeUlio and buying records
summary: His high school band director's rotating lessons, Glenn Drewes, and his paper route money spent on records.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: We should get his name on the record.

DeUlio. Large D, small E, Large I — L-I-O. U-I-L-O. DeUlio. And I mean I think of him almost every day, still. Because he was just remarkable, a remarkable person you know. And he would say — anytime I had time I was in the band room practicing. During lunch I would eat lunch in 10 minutes and I’d go over to the band room and practice. And that’s just what I did. And he had one of those rotating lesson schedules so that he could have the groups of kids that played the same part, he could work with them and teach them, you know give a little more instruction than just playing in band and not getting the part. You know what I mean? So he had a rotating schedule and so if I came down there and there was a group in there he’d go, “Go teach the saxophones, go teach the alto saxophones.” And I’d say, “I can’t teach them, their music is in a different key.” “Well you’ll get it, don’t worry about it.” That’s all the instruction. ‘Cause, and then the next guy, you know who Glen Drews is?

Okay he sat right here in high school band. We were together. You know? And we were pretty good. And then the third guy, he could barely play a G on top of the staff. He was one of the first trumpets too. And then the guy that was the fourth one — it was better that you didn’t hear him. You know? But he understood why every person was in band. © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

That was his forte, besides playing trumpet. He played trumpet. I didn’t take lessons from him ‘cause — he would have probably given me lessons but I didn’t really have any money. We were poor you know and I had a paper route and I bought records with that money. That’s what I did. Every day when we finished when I had collected the money for the papers I knew how much I had to pay for the papers and I knew how much was left. And I’d go directly to Abraham & Strauss. Abraham & Strauss was a department store in Long Island and it probably is other places. But they had a record department. Unheard of today. But I would go there and I’d look through the instrumental section.

And I’d find — oh look there’s a new Harry James record. I’ve got to have this. You know and then the record collection kept — and when I gave away my records, except for the ones that are sort of collectors’ things for me I had over 800 of those. I have way over a thousand CDs. And now, with all the digital stuff, I don’t even know what I have. I have 15,000 pieces of music that are catalogued.
